hints: Fix the first player?s card order to 1..n; every relative order of the second player occurs for exactly n! pairs of card orders.
Tied rounds are fixed points of the relative permutation. Delete those rows and cards: the remaining derangement keeps the same greater-than comparisons.
Count derangements by the number of excedances using inclusion?exclusion over fixed points and Eulerian numbers.
analogy: First choose a relative permutation; fixed points are ties, and the remaining positions split into wins for each player.
example: For n=3 and scores a=1,b=2, there are no ties. Exactly one derangement has two excedances, so the answer is 3!?1=6 possible pairs of card orders.
algorithm: Let j=n-a-b. If j<0, the answer is 0. Let E[s][e] be the number of permutations of s elements with e excedances (positions i where ?(i)>i), with E[0][0]=1 and E[s][e]=(e+1)E[s-1][e]+(s-e)E[s-1][e-1]. Let D[m][e]=?(i=0..m)(-1)^i C(m,i)E[m-i][e], the number of derangements with e excedances. For m=a+b, the answer is n!?C(n,j)?D[m][b] modulo 1,000,000,007. Precompute E through the largest n; evaluate D for each test in O(m) using factorials and inverse factorials for binomial coefficients.
correctness: Every first-player order can be relabeled as 1..n, leaving n! choices that all have the same relative comparison pattern. A tie is exactly a fixed point, so selecting its j positions and deleting them leaves a derangement on m=n-j elements; deleting a fixed point preserves the comparison direction of every remaining position. The second player wins exactly at excedances, so D[m][b] counts the possible tie-free relative orders. Inclusion?exclusion removes all fixed points from Eulerian permutations, and choosing the j tie positions gives C(n,j). Multiplying these independent counts yields exactly all games with scores (a,b).
complexity: Precomputation takes O(N?) time and space for Eulerian numbers through N=max n. Each test takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space, where n is that test?s card count.
